chapters.title: Book Two (1805) — Chapter I
paragraphs: Prince Andrew was leaving the next evening. The old prince, never one to break his routine, had retired after dinner as usual. The little princess was in her sister-in-law's room. Prince Andrew, wearing a traveling coat without epaulettes, had been packing with his valet in the rooms set aside for him. After inspecting the carriage himself and watching the trunks being loaded, he ordered the horses harnessed. Only the things he always kept with him remained in his room: a small box, a large canteen fitted with silver tableware, two Turkish pistols, and a saber — a gift from his father, who had brought it back from the siege of Ochakov. All of Prince Andrew's traveling things were in perfect order: new, clean, and wrapped in cloth covers carefully tied with tape.

When setting out on a journey or changing their way of life, thoughtful people generally fall into a serious mood. At such moments a person reviews the past and plans for the future. Prince Andrew's face looked deeply thoughtful and tender. With his hands behind his back, he paced briskly from corner to corner of the room, staring straight ahead and shaking his head in thought. Was he afraid of going to war, or sad about leaving his wife? Perhaps both — but clearly he didn't want to be seen in that state, because when he heard footsteps in the corridor he quickly unclasped his hands, stopped by a table as though tying the cover of his small box, and put on his usual calm, impenetrable expression. It was the heavy tread of Princess Mary.

"I hear you've ordered the horses harnessed," she said breathlessly — she had obviously been running. "And I wanted so much to talk with you alone one more time! God knows how long we'll be apart. You're not angry that I came? You've changed so much, Andrusha," she added, as if to explain her question.

She smiled as she used his pet name, "Andrusha." It was clearly strange for her to think that this stern, handsome man was the same Andrusha — the skinny, mischievous boy she had played with as a child.
"And where is Lise?" he asked, answering her question with nothing more than a smile.

"She was so tired she fell asleep on the sofa in my room. Oh, Andrew! What a treasure of a wife you have," she said, sitting down on the sofa facing her brother. "She's practically a child — such a dear, cheerful child. I've grown so fond of her."
Prince Andrew said nothing, but the princess caught the look of irony and contempt that crossed his face.

"We should be patient with small weaknesses — who doesn't have them, Andrew? Don't forget she was raised in high society, so her position now is hardly an easy one. We should try to understand everyone's situation. To understand all is to forgive all. Think what it must be like for her, poor thing — after the life she was used to — to be separated from her husband and left alone in the country, and in her condition. It's very hard."
Prince Andrew smiled at his sister the way we smile at people we think we understand completely.
"You live in the country and don't find it terrible," he replied.

"That's... different. Why talk about me? I don't want any other life, and couldn't have one, because I've never known anything else. But think, Andrew — a young society woman buried in the country during the best years of her life, all alone. Papa is always busy, and I... well, you know how little I have to offer in the way of entertainment to a woman used to the finest company. There's only Mademoiselle Bourienne..."
"I don't like your Mademoiselle Bourienne at all," said Prince Andrew.

"Really? She's very kind and nice, and above all, she deserves pity. She has no one — no one at all. To tell the truth, I don't really need her, and she's even a bit in my way. You know I've always been something of a loner, and I'm even more so now. I like being alone... Father likes her very much. She and Mikhail Ivanovich are the two people he's always gentle and kind to, because he's been a benefactor to both of them. As Sterne says: 'We don't love people so much for the good they've done us as for the good we've done them.' Father took her in when she was left homeless after her own father died. She's very good-natured, and Father likes the way she reads. She reads aloud to him in the evenings, and she does it beautifully."
"Let me be frank, Mary — I'd guess Father's personality makes things difficult for you sometimes, doesn't it?" Prince Andrew asked suddenly.
Princess Mary was first surprised, then horrified by the question.
"Difficult for me? For me?... Difficult for me!" she stammered.
"He was always rather harsh, and I'd imagine he's become quite trying now," said Prince Andrew, apparently speaking lightly about their father to test his sister.

"You are good in every way, Andrew, but you have a kind of intellectual pride," the princess said, following her own train of thought rather than the thread of the conversation, "and that's a great sin. How can anyone judge Father? And even if someone could, what feeling other than reverence could a man like our father inspire? I am so content and happy with him. I only wish all of you were as happy as I am."
Her brother shook his head, unconvinced.

"The only thing that's hard for me — I'll tell you the truth, Andrew — is Father's attitude toward religion. I can't understand how a man of his extraordinary intellect can fail to see what's as clear as day, and can go so far astray. That's the only thing that makes me unhappy. But even in this, I've noticed a slight improvement lately. His sarcasm about it has been less bitter recently, and he received a monk the other day and had a long conversation with him."
"Oh, my dear — I'm afraid you and your monk are wasting your ammunition," said Prince Andrew with a teasing but affectionate tone.
"Oh, my dear friend, I only pray and hope that God will hear me. Andrew..." she said timidly after a moment of silence, "I have a great favor to ask of you."
"What is it, dear?"

"No — promise you won't refuse! It won't cause you any trouble and it's nothing beneath you, but it would comfort me. Promise, Andrusha!" she said, reaching into her handbag but not yet taking out whatever she was holding, as if the object itself were the request and couldn't be shown until the promise was made.
She looked at her brother timidly.
"Even if it were a great deal of trouble..." Prince Andrew replied, seeming to guess what it was about.

"Think whatever you want! I know you're just like Father. Think what you like, but do this for my sake! Please! Father's father — our grandfather — wore it through all his wars." She still hadn't taken out what was in her handbag. "So you promise?"
"Of course. What is it?"
"Andrew, I want to bless you with this icon, and you must promise never to take it off. Do you promise?"

"As long as it doesn't weigh a hundred pounds and break my neck... To please you..." said Prince Andrew. But seeing immediately the pained expression his joke had brought to his sister's face, he caught himself and added: "I'm glad — really, dear, I'm very glad."

"Against your will He will save you and show you mercy and bring you to Himself, for in Him alone is truth and peace," she said in a voice trembling with emotion, solemnly holding up before her brother with both hands a small, oval, antique icon of the Savior with a dark face in a gold setting, on a finely wrought silver chain.
She crossed herself, kissed the icon, and handed it to Andrew.
"Please, Andrew, for my sake!"

Rays of gentle light shone from her large, timid eyes. Those eyes illuminated her whole thin, sickly face and made it beautiful. Her brother reached for the icon, but she stopped him. Andrew understood — he crossed himself and kissed it. His expression held tenderness, for he was genuinely moved, but also a glint of irony.
"Thank you, my dear." She kissed him on the forehead and sat back down on the sofa. They were silent for a moment.

"As I was saying, Andrew — be kind and generous, the way you always used to be. Don't judge Lise too harshly," she began again. "She's so sweet, so good-natured, and her situation right now is very hard."
"I don't recall complaining about my wife to you, Masha, or blaming her. Why are you saying all this?"
Red blotches appeared on Princess Mary's face, and she fell silent as though she felt guilty.
"I said nothing to you, but others have already spoken to you about it. And that makes me sorry," he continued.

The blotches deepened on her forehead, neck, and cheeks. She tried to speak but couldn't. Her brother had guessed correctly: the little princess had been crying after dinner, talking about her fears regarding her pregnancy and how much she dreaded it, complaining about her fate, her father-in-law, and her husband. After crying, she had fallen asleep. Prince Andrew felt sorry for his sister.

"Listen, Masha — I have nothing to reproach my wife with, and I never have, and I never will. And I have nothing to reproach myself with toward her either — and it will always be that way, no matter what circumstances I find myself in. But if you want the truth... if you want to know whether I'm happy? No. Is she happy? No. But why it's so — I don't know..."

As he said this he stood up, went to his sister, and bent down to kiss her forehead. His fine eyes lit up with a thoughtful, kind brightness that was rare for him, but he was looking not at his sister — he was gazing past her, over her head, into the darkness of the open doorway.

"Let's go to her — I need to say goodbye. Or else go wake her, and I'll come in a moment. Petrusha!" he called to his valet. "Come here, take these things. Put this on the seat and this on the right side."

Princess Mary got up and moved toward the door, then stopped and said: "Andrew, if you had faith, you would have turned to God and asked Him to give you the love you don't feel, and your prayer would have been answered."
"Well — maybe!" said Prince Andrew. "Go on, Masha. I'll come right away."

On the way to his sister's room, in the corridor connecting one wing of the house to the other, Prince Andrew ran into Mademoiselle Bourienne, who was smiling sweetly. It was the third time that day she had appeared before him with that ecstatic, seemingly artless smile in some secluded passageway.
"Oh! I thought you were in your room," she said, blushing for some reason and dropping her eyes.

Prince Andrew looked at her coldly, and an expression of anger suddenly crossed his face. He said nothing, but stared at her forehead and hair without meeting her eyes, with such contempt that the Frenchwoman blushed and slipped away without a word. When he reached his sister's room, his wife was already awake, and her cheerful voice, words tumbling out one after another, came through the open door. She was speaking in French, as always, and as if after a long period of self-restraint she was trying to make up for lost time.
"No, but imagine old Countess Zubova with those fake curls and her mouth full of false teeth, as if she were trying to cheat old age... Ha, ha, ha! Mary!"

Prince Andrew had already heard this exact sentence about Countess Zubova, and the same laugh, from his wife about five times in the company of others. He entered the room quietly. The little princess — plump and rosy — was sitting in an easy chair with her needlework in her hands, chattering away, repeating reminiscences and pet phrases from Petersburg. Prince Andrew came up, stroked her hair, and asked if she felt rested after the journey. She answered and went on talking.

A coach drawn by six horses stood waiting at the front steps. It was an autumn night, so dark the coachman couldn't see the carriage pole. Servants carrying lanterns bustled around the entrance. The enormous house blazed with light pouring through its tall windows. The household servants were crowded in the front hall, waiting to say goodbye to the young prince. Everyone was gathered in the reception room: Mikhail Ivanovich, Mademoiselle Bourienne, Princess Mary, and the little princess. Prince Andrew had been called to his father's study — the old man wanted to say goodbye in private. They were all waiting for the two of them to come out.
When Prince Andrew entered the study, the old man was sitting at his desk in the old-fashioned spectacles and white dressing gown he wore for no one but his son, writing. He glanced up.
"Leaving?" And he went back to his writing.
"I've come to say goodbye."
"Kiss me here." He pointed to his cheek. "Thank you. Thank you!"
"What are you thanking me for?"

"For not wasting time and not hanging on to a woman's apron strings. Duty comes first. Thank you, thank you!" And he went on writing, his pen sputtering and squeaking. "If you have something to say, say it. I can do two things at once," he added.
"About my wife... I feel bad enough as it is, leaving her in your care..."
"Stop talking nonsense. Say what you mean."
"When it's time for her to give birth, send to Moscow for a doctor. Have him come here."
The old prince stopped writing and stared at his son with stern eyes, as if he didn't understand.

"I know that if nature doesn't do its work, no one can help," said Prince Andrew, obviously uncomfortable. "I know that out of a million cases, only one goes badly. But it's what she wants, and what I want too. People have been telling her things. She had a dream and she's frightened."
"Hmm... hmm..." the old prince muttered to himself as he finished what he was writing. "I'll take care of it."
He signed with a flourish, then suddenly turned to his son and laughed.
"It's a bad situation, isn't it?"
"What's bad, Father?"
"The wife!" the old prince said, brief and pointed.
"I don't understand!" said Prince Andrew.
"There's nothing to be done about it, son," the prince said. "They're all the same — you can't un-marry. Don't worry, I won't tell anyone. But you know it yourself."
He seized his son's hand with his small, bony fingers, shook it, stared straight into his face with sharp eyes that seemed to see right through him, and laughed again — that cold laugh of his.

The son sighed, silently admitting that his father had understood him. The old man went on folding and sealing his letter, snatching up the wax, the seal, and the paper and tossing them aside with his usual rapid movements.
"What can you do? She's pretty! I'll take care of everything. Set your mind at ease," he said in short, clipped phrases as he sealed the letter.
Andrew said nothing; he was both glad and uneasy that his father understood him. The old man stood and handed the letter to his son.

"Listen," he said. "Don't worry about your wife — what can be done will be done. Now listen: give this letter to Mikhail Ilarionovich. I've written that he should put you to good use in real assignments and not keep you stuck as an adjutant — it's a dead-end position. Tell him I remember him and think well of him. And write to tell me how he receives you. If he treats you well, serve him. A son of Nikolai Bolkonsky doesn't need to serve under anyone who's out of favor. Now come here."

He spoke so fast he didn't finish half his words, but his son was used to understanding him. He led Andrew to the desk, raised the lid, pulled open a drawer, and took out an exercise book filled with his bold, tall, dense handwriting.

"I'll probably die before you do. So remember — these are my memoirs. Give them to the Emperor after I'm gone. Now here's a government bond and a letter — it's a prize for whoever writes a history of Suvorov's campaigns. Send it to the Academy. And here are some notes for you to read after I'm dead. You'll find them useful."
Andrew did not tell his father he would surely live many more years. He felt he shouldn't say it.
"I'll do it all, Father," he said.

"Very well. Now — goodbye!" He held out his hand for his son to kiss, then embraced him. "Remember this, Prince Andrew: if they kill you, it will grieve me — your old father..." He paused abruptly, then in a shrill, cracking voice suddenly cried out: "But if I learn that you did not conduct yourself as a son of Nikolai Bolkonsky, I will be ashamed!"
"You didn't need to say that, Father," the son replied with a smile.
The old man was silent.
"I also wanted to ask you," Prince Andrew continued, "if I'm killed and if I have a son — don't let him be taken away from you, as I mentioned yesterday. Let him grow up with you... Please."
"Not let the wife have him?" said the old man, and laughed.
They stood facing each other in silence. The old man's sharp eyes were fixed on his son's. Something twitched in the lower part of the old prince's face.
"We've said goodbye. Go!" he shouted suddenly in a loud, angry voice, and flung the door open.

"What is it? What's wrong?" both princesses exclaimed when they caught a momentary glimpse at the doorway of Prince Andrew and the old man behind him — white dressing gown, spectacles, no wig — shouting in an angry voice.
Prince Andrew sighed and said nothing.
"Well!" he said, turning to his wife.
And the way he said "Well!" was coldly ironic, as if to say: Now go ahead with your performance.
"Andrew — already!" said the little princess, turning pale and looking at her husband with alarm.
He embraced her. She cried out and fainted against his shoulder.
He carefully freed the shoulder she was leaning on, looked into her face, and gently settled her into an armchair.
"Goodbye, Mary," he said softly to his sister, taking her hand and kissing it, and then he walked out of the room with quick steps.

The little princess lay in the armchair while Mademoiselle Bourienne rubbed her temples. Princess Mary, still holding her sister-in-law's arm, gazed with her beautiful, tear-filled eyes at the door through which Prince Andrew had gone and made the sign of the cross in his direction. From the study, like pistol shots, came the repeated sound of the old man furiously blowing his nose. The moment Prince Andrew left, the study door flew open and the stern figure of the old man in his white dressing gown appeared.
"Gone? Good!" he said. And glancing angrily at the unconscious little princess, he shook his head in disapproval and slammed the door.

chapters.title: Book Two (1805) — Chapter II
paragraphs: In October 1805, a Russian army was occupying the villages and towns of the Archduchy of Austria, while fresh regiments still arriving from Russia were settling around the fortress of Braunau and burdening the local residents on whom they were billeted. Braunau served as the headquarters of the commander in chief, Kutuzov.

On October 11, 1805, one of the infantry regiments that had just reached Braunau was halted half a mile from town, waiting to be inspected by the commander in chief. Despite the distinctly un-Russian landscape — fruit orchards, stone fences, tiled roofs, and hills in the distance — and despite the fact that the curious locals staring at the soldiers were not Russian, the regiment looked exactly like any Russian regiment preparing for inspection anywhere in the heart of Russia.

The evening before, an order had come down that the commander in chief would inspect the regiment while on the march. Although the wording was unclear to the regimental commander — there was some question about whether the troops should be in marching order or not — a conference of battalion commanders decided to present the regiment in full parade formation, on the principle that it's always better to bow too low than not low enough. So after a twenty-mile march, the soldiers were kept up all night mending and polishing without a moment's sleep, while adjutants and company commanders calculated and recounted, and by morning the regiment — instead of the straggling, disorderly mob it had been on its march the day before — presented a well-ordered display of two thousand men, each of whom knew his place and his duty, with every button and every strap in position, shining with cleanliness. And not only was the exterior in order; had the commander in chief cared to look beneath the uniforms, he would have found a clean shirt on every man and in every knapsack the regulation number of articles — "needle, soap, and all," as the soldiers liked to say. There was only one problem no one could solve: the state of the men's boots. More than half were full of holes. But this wasn't the regimental commander's fault — he had submitted repeated requests, and the Austrian commissariat had simply never delivered the boots. The regiment had marched some seven hundred miles.

The regimental commander was an elderly, hot-tempered, heavyset general with grizzled eyebrows and whiskers, broader from chest to back than across the shoulders. He wore a brand-new uniform still showing its fold creases and thick gold epaulettes that seemed to stand up rather than lie flat on his massive shoulders. He had the air of a man happily performing one of the most solemn duties of his life. He walked back and forth in front of the ranks, pulling himself up and slightly arching his back at every step. It was clear the commander adored his regiment, took immense pride in it, and thought of nothing else — yet his strutting walk also suggested that military matters were not the only thing on his mind, and that social life and the fair sex occupied no small corner of his thoughts.

"Well, Mikhail Mitrich, sir?" he said, addressing one of the battalion commanders, who pressed forward with a smile. It was obvious they were both in high spirits. "We had our hands full last night. Still, I'd say the regiment doesn't look half bad, eh?"
The battalion commander caught the good-humored irony and laughed.
"It wouldn't be turned off the field even on the Tsaritsin parade ground."
"What's that?" asked the commander.
At that moment, two horsemen appeared on the road from town, where lookouts had been posted. They were an aide-de-camp and a Cossack riding behind him.

The aide-de-camp had been sent to clarify the previous day's ambiguously worded order: the commander in chief wanted to see the regiment exactly as it had been on the march — in greatcoats and packs, without any preparation whatsoever.

An official from the Hofkriegsrath in Vienna had visited Kutuzov the previous day with proposals and demands that he join forces with the army of Archduke Ferdinand and Mack. Kutuzov, who considered this merger inadvisable, intended — among other arguments in support of his position — to show the Austrian general the wretched condition in which the troops arrived from Russia. For this purpose he wanted to meet the regiment in its actual state; the worse it looked, the happier the commander in chief would be. Though the aide-de-camp didn't know these background details, he delivered the definite order: the men were to be in greatcoats and marching order, and the commander in chief would be displeased otherwise. Hearing this, the regimental commander hung his head, shrugged silently, and threw out his arms in frustration.
"A fine mess we've made of it!" he said.

"Didn't I tell you, Mikhail Mitrich? When they said 'on the march,' it meant in greatcoats!" he said reproachfully to the battalion commander. "Oh, my God!" He stepped forward decisively. "Company commanders!" he bellowed in a voice built for commanding. "Sergeants major!... How soon will he be here?" he asked the aide-de-camp with a respectful politeness clearly directed at the personage in question.
"An hour, I'd say."
"Will we have time to change?"
"I couldn't say, General."

The regimental commander walked up to the line himself and ordered the soldiers to change into their greatcoats. Company commanders ran to their companies, sergeants major began scrambling — the greatcoats weren't in the best shape — and instantly the silent, orderly squares began to sway, stretch, and buzz with voices. Soldiers ran in every direction, tossing their knapsacks up with a jerk of the shoulders, pulling straps over their heads, unbuckling overcoats and jamming their arms through the sleeves.

Within half an hour, everything was back in order — only the squares had turned from black to gray. The regimental commander walked with his jerky steps to the front and surveyed the whole formation from a distance.
"What in the — what is this? This!" he shouted, stopping short. "Commander of the third company!"

"Commander of the third company — the general wants you!... Commander to the general... third company to the commander!" The words passed down the lines, and an adjutant ran off to find the missing officer.

When the eager but garbled message finally reached its destination as "The general to the third company!" the missing officer appeared from behind his men and — though he was a middle-aged man not accustomed to running — came trotting awkwardly toward the general, stumbling on his toes. The captain's face wore the anxious look of a schoolboy called on to recite a lesson he hasn't learned. Spots bloomed on his nose, whose redness was clearly the result of heavy drinking, and his mouth twitched nervously. The general looked him up and down as he arrived, panting and slowing his pace.

"You'll be dressing your men in petticoats next! What is this?" the regimental commander barked, jutting his jaw toward a soldier in the third company's ranks who wore a greatcoat of bluish cloth that stood out from all the others. "What have you been doing? The commander in chief is about to arrive and you abandon your post? I'll teach you to put fancy coats on your men for inspection!"
The company commander pressed two fingers ever harder to his cap visor, as if all his salvation lay in that gesture.
"Well? Why don't you answer? Who's that you've got dressed up like a Hungarian?" the commander demanded with grim sarcasm.
"Your excellency..."
"Well? 'Your excellency' what? 'Your excellency'! Nobody seems to know anything around here."
"Your excellency, it's the officer Dolokhov, who was reduced to the ranks," the captain said quietly.
"So? Has he been demoted to field marshal, or to private? If he's a private, he wears regulation uniform like everyone else."
"Your excellency, you gave him permission yourself, on the march."

"Permission? Permission? That's just like you young officers," the regimental commander said, cooling off slightly. "Permission, indeed... You say one word to any of you and then... What?" he added, his irritation flaring again. "I'm asking you to dress your men properly."

He turned to the adjutant and continued down the line with his jerky stride. He was clearly enjoying his own display of anger and looking for another target. Having snapped at one officer over an unpolished badge and at another for a crooked line, he reached the third company.
"How are you standing? Where's your leg? Your leg!" the commander bellowed in a pained voice, though he was still five men away from Dolokhov in his bluish-gray coat.
Dolokhov slowly straightened his bent knee, staring directly at the general's face with clear, insolent eyes.
"Why a blue coat? Take it off... Sergeant major! Change his coat — the ras—" He didn't finish.
"General, I must follow orders, but I am not required to endure —" Dolokhov cut in sharply.
"No talking in the ranks! No talking!"
"— insults," Dolokhov finished, his voice loud, clear, and ringing.
The general's eyes met the soldier's. The general fell silent, tugging angrily at his tight collar.
"I would ask you to kindly change your coat," he said as he turned and walked away.

chapters.title: Book Two (1805) — Chapter III
paragraphs: "He's coming!" shouted the lookout at that moment.

The regimental commander, flushing red, ran to his horse, seized the stirrup with trembling hands, threw himself across the saddle, righted himself, drew his saber, and with a happy, determined expression, his mouth opening crookedly, prepared to shout. The regiment stirred like a bird ruffling its feathers, then went perfectly still.
"Atten-TION!" the regimental commander roared in a voice that shook the soul — a voice expressing joy for himself, severity for the regiment, and welcome for the approaching commander.

Down the broad country road, bordered on both sides by trees, came a tall, light-blue Viennese carriage, creaking faintly on its springs and pulled by six horses at a brisk trot. Behind it galloped the staff officers and a convoy of Croatian soldiers. Kutuzov sat beside an Austrian general in a white uniform that looked out of place among the Russian black ones. The carriage halted before the regiment. Kutuzov and the Austrian spoke in low voices, and Kutuzov gave a slight smile as he stepped heavily down from the carriage — as if those two thousand soldiers holding their breath to watch him, and the regimental commander himself, simply didn't exist.

The command rang out, and again the regiment shivered with a jingling sound as it presented arms. Then in the dead silence the commander in chief's faint voice was heard. The regiment roared: "Long life to Your Excel-len-lency!" Then all was silent again. At first Kutuzov stood still while the regiment marched past; then he and the general in white, accompanied by the staff, walked between the ranks.

From the way the regimental commander saluted the commander in chief and devoured him with his eyes, drawing himself up obsequiously — from the way he walked behind the generals through the ranks, bowing forward and barely able to restrain his jerky movements — from the way he leaped at every word or gesture from the commander in chief — it was clear he performed his duties as a subordinate with even greater enthusiasm than his duties as a commander. Thanks to his strictness and dedication, the regiment was in excellent shape compared to others that had arrived in Braunau at the same time. Only 217 men were sick or missing. Everything was in fine order — except the boots.

Kutuzov walked through the ranks, occasionally stopping to say a few friendly words to officers he had known from the Turkish campaign, and sometimes to the common soldiers as well. Looking at their boots, he shook his head sadly several times, pointing them out to the Austrian general with an expression that seemed to say he wasn't blaming anyone but couldn't help noticing how bad things were. The regimental commander rushed forward each time, afraid of missing a single word the commander in chief might say about the regiment. About twenty staff officers followed behind Kutuzov at a distance that let them hear every quietly spoken word. These men talked among themselves and sometimes laughed. Walking closest to the commander in chief was a handsome adjutant — Prince Bolkonsky. Beside him was his friend Nesvitsky, a tall, extremely stout staff officer with a kind, smiling, handsome face and moist eyes. Nesvitsky could barely contain his laughter, which was being provoked by a swarthy hussar officer walking alongside him. This hussar, his face perfectly serious, without the faintest smile or change in his fixed expression, watched the regimental commander's back and mimicked his every movement. Each time the commander lurched forward, the hussar lurched forward in exactly the same way. Nesvitsky laughed and nudged the others to watch.

Kutuzov walked slowly and heavily past thousands of eyes bulging from their sockets to see their commander. When he reached the third company, he suddenly stopped. His staff, not expecting this, crowded in closer behind him.
"Ah, Timokhin!" he said, recognizing the red-nosed captain who had been called out over the blue greatcoat.

It would have seemed impossible for anyone to stand more rigidly at attention than Timokhin had when the regimental commander reprimanded him, but now that the commander in chief addressed him, the captain drew himself up so stiffly it seemed he couldn't have held it a second longer. Kutuzov clearly understood the man's situation and wished him well, so he quickly turned away, a barely perceptible smile crossing his scarred, puffy face.
"Another Ismail veteran," he remarked. "A brave officer! Are you satisfied with him?" he asked the regimental commander.
The regimental commander — unaware that behind him the hussar was mirroring him like a looking glass — snapped forward and answered: "Very satisfied, Your Excellency!"
"We all have our weaknesses," said Kutuzov with a smile, walking on. "He used to be a bit too fond of Bacchus."

The regimental commander was afraid he was being criticized and said nothing. At that moment, the hussar noticed the red-nosed captain's face and sucked-in stomach and mimicked his expression and posture so perfectly that Nesvitsky couldn't help bursting out laughing. Kutuzov turned around. The hussar evidently had complete control of his face — in the instant Kutuzov was turning, he managed to pull a grimace and then snap back to a perfectly serious, deferential, innocent expression.
The third company was the last, and Kutuzov paused, apparently trying to remember something. Prince Andrew stepped forward from the staff and said in French:
[speaking in French] "You asked me to remind you about the officer Dolokhov, reduced to the ranks in this regiment."
"Where is Dolokhov?" Kutuzov asked.

Dolokhov, who had already changed into a soldier's gray greatcoat, didn't wait to be summoned. The well-built, fair-haired soldier with his clear blue eyes stepped forward from the ranks, walked up to the commander in chief, and presented arms.
"Do you have a complaint?" Kutuzov asked, frowning slightly.
"This is Dolokhov," said Prince Andrew.
"Ah!" said Kutuzov. "I hope this will be a lesson for you. Do your duty. The Emperor is merciful, and I won't forget you if you prove yourself."

Those clear blue eyes looked up at the commander in chief just as boldly as they had stared down the regimental commander — as if their gaze could tear away the veil of protocol that separates a commander in chief from a common soldier.

"One thing I ask of Your Excellency," Dolokhov said in his firm, ringing, deliberate voice. "I ask for the opportunity to redeem my fault and prove my devotion to His Majesty the Emperor and to Russia!"

Kutuzov turned away. The same smile flickered in his eyes — the one he'd shown when turning from Captain Timokhin. He turned with a grimace, as if to say that everything Dolokhov had told him, and anything he could possibly say, had long been known, that it all wearied him, and that this was not at all what he wanted. He walked away and got into the carriage.
The regiment broke into companies and marched to their assigned quarters near Braunau, where they hoped to receive boots and clothing and to rest after their grueling marches.

"You won't hold it against me, Prokhor Ignatych?" said the regimental commander, catching up with the third company on its way to quarters and riding up alongside Captain Timokhin, who was walking at the front. The commander's face was now beaming with irrepressible delight, the inspection safely behind him. "It comes with serving the Emperor... sometimes you're a bit sharp on parade. I'm the first to apologize — you know me! He was very pleased!" He extended his hand to the captain.

"Don't mention it, General — as if I'd dare take offense!" the captain replied, his nose growing redder as he smiled, revealing the gap where two front teeth had been knocked out by a rifle butt at Ismail.
"And please tell Mr. Dolokhov I won't forget him — he can rest easy. Oh, and tell me — I've been meaning to ask — how is he behaving himself? And in general..."
"In terms of service, he's quite meticulous, Your Excellency. But his temperament..." said Timokhin.
"What about his temperament?" the commander asked.
"It changes from day to day," the captain answered. "Some days he's sensible, educated, and perfectly pleasant. Other days he's a wild animal. In Poland, he nearly killed a Jew."
"Well, well," the regimental commander remarked. "Still, one should feel for a young man in his situation. He has important connections, after all... So you'll just..."
"I will, Your Excellency," said Timokhin, his smile showing he understood exactly what the commander was getting at.
"Good, good!"
The regimental commander found Dolokhov in the ranks and, pulling up his horse, said to him:
"After the next engagement — epaulettes."
Dolokhov glanced back but said nothing. The mocking smile on his lips didn't change.

"Well, that's that," the commander continued. "A cup of vodka for every man — from me," he added loud enough for the soldiers to hear. "Thank you all! God be praised!" And he rode past the company to catch up with the next.
"He really is a good man — you can serve under someone like that," Timokhin said to the subaltern beside him.
"In a word — a real King of Hearts," the subaltern replied with a laugh, using the regimental commander's well-known nickname.
The cheerful mood of the officers after the inspection was catching, and the soldiers marched on in high spirits. Voices could be heard on every side.
"They said Kutuzov was blind in one eye?"
"That's right! Completely blind!"
"No way, friend — he sees better than you do. Boots and leg wraps... he spotted everything."
"When he looked down at my feet, friend... well, I thought..."
"And that other one with him, the Austrian — looked like he was covered in chalk, white as flour! Bet they polish him up like a cannon."
"Hey, Fedeshen! Did he say when the fighting starts? You were right near him. Everyone's saying Bonaparte himself is at Braunau."

"Bonaparte himself! Listen to this fool, the things he comes up with! The Prussians are mobilizing now. The Austrians are putting them down, see. Once they're dealt with, then the war with Bonaparte begins. And he says Bonaparte's in Braunau! Shows you're an idiot. You should listen more carefully!"
"Damn these quartermasters! Look — fifth company's already turning into the village. They'll have their porridge cooked before we even reach our billets."
"Give me a biscuit, you devil!"
"And did you give me tobacco yesterday? That's what I thought, friend! Well, fine — here you go."
"They should call a halt here, or we'll end up doing another four miles on an empty stomach."
"Wasn't it great when those Germans gave us rides? You just sit there and get pulled along."
"Out here, friend, the people are dirt poor. Back there they were at least Poles — still under Russian rule — but here they're all proper Germans."
"Singers to the front!" came the captain's order.

About twenty men ran out from the ranks to the front. The lead drummer turned to face the singers and, waving his arm, launched into a long, drawn-out soldiers' song that began with "Morning dawned, the sun was rising" and ended with "Onward, brothers, on to glory, led by Father Kamensky." The song had been written during the Turkish campaign, and the only change now that they were in Austria was that "Father Kamensky" had been swapped for "Father Kutuzov."

Having belted out those final words with a soldier's gusto and flung his arms down as though hurling something to the ground, the drummer — a lean, handsome soldier of about forty — glared sternly at the other singers and narrowed his eyes. Satisfied that all eyes were on him, he raised both arms as if lifting some invisible but precious object above his head, held it there for several seconds, then suddenly threw it down and began:
"Oh, my bower, oh, my bower...!"

"Oh, my bower new...!" echoed twenty voices, and the man with the castanets, despite the weight of his full kit, rushed to the front and walked backward before the company, shaking his shoulders and rattling his castanets as if threatening someone. The soldiers swung their arms in time and marched with long, easy strides. Behind the company came the sound of wheels, creaking springs, and horses' hooves — Kutuzov and his staff were heading back to town. The commander in chief signaled for the men to continue at ease, and everyone in his party showed pleasure at the sound of the singing, the dancing soldier, and the smartly marching men. In the second file from the right flank, where the carriage was passing, one soldier drew attention even without meaning to — a blue-eyed man marching with particular grace and confidence in time to the song, looking at those riding past as if he pitied anyone who wasn't marching with the company at that moment. It was Dolokhov. The hussar cornet from Kutuzov's staff — the same one who had been mimicking the regimental commander — dropped back from the carriage and rode up alongside Dolokhov.

Hussar cornet Zherkov had once belonged to the wild crowd Dolokhov led in Petersburg. He had run into Dolokhov abroad after his demotion and hadn't bothered to acknowledge him. But now that Kutuzov had spoken to the gentleman ranker, Zherkov addressed him with the warmth of an old friend.
"My dear fellow, how are you?" he called out over the singing, keeping his horse in step with the company.
"How am I?" Dolokhov answered coldly. "As you see."
The upbeat song gave a special flavor both to Zherkov's breezy familiarity and to the deliberate chill in Dolokhov's reply.
"And how do you get along with the officers?" Zherkov asked.
"Fine. They're decent men. And how did you manage to worm your way onto the staff?"
"I was assigned — I'm on duty."
Both fell silent.

"She let the hawk fly upward from her wide right sleeve," the song went on, stirring an instinctive feeling of courage and high spirits. Their conversation would probably have gone differently if not for the effect of that song.
"Is it true the Austrians have been beaten?" asked Dolokhov.
"Who the hell knows. That's what they say."
"Good," Dolokhov answered, brief and sharp, as the rhythm of the song demanded.
"Listen, come around some evening — we'll play some faro!" said Zherkov.
"What, you have too much money?"
"Come on."
"I can't. I've sworn off. I won't drink or gamble until I get my commission back."
"Well, that's only until the first battle."
"We'll see."
They fell silent again.
"Drop by if you ever need anything. At least the staff can be useful for something..."
Dolokhov smiled. "Don't bother. If I want something, I won't beg for it — I'll take it."
"Well, I didn't mean —"
"And I only —"
"Goodbye."
"Stay well."
"It's a long, long way — to my native land..."

Zherkov touched his spurs to his horse. It pranced excitedly, unsure which foot to start with, then found its stride and galloped past the company to catch up with the carriage, still keeping time to the song.

chapters.title: Book Two (1805) — Chapter IV
paragraphs: Returning from the review, Kutuzov brought the Austrian general to his private room and, calling for his adjutant, asked for papers on the condition of the arriving troops and the letters that had come from Archduke Ferdinand, who commanded the advance army. Prince Andrew Bolkonsky entered the room with the requested documents. Kutuzov and the Austrian member of the Hofkriegsrath were sitting at a table with a map spread out before them.
[speaking in French] "Ah..." said Kutuzov, glancing at Bolkonsky as though asking the adjutant to wait, and went on speaking in French.

[speaking in French] "All I can say, General," he began with an elegant pleasantness of tone and delivery that made you want to listen to each carefully chosen word — it was clear Kutuzov enjoyed the sound of his own voice — "all I can say, General, is that if the matter depended solely on my personal wishes, His Majesty Emperor Francis's will would have been fulfilled long ago. I would have joined the Archduke without delay. And believe me, on my honor, it would be a genuine pleasure for me to hand over supreme command of the army to a more knowledgeable and capable general — of whom Austria has so many — and to lay down this heavy burden of responsibility. But circumstances are sometimes stronger than we are, General."

Kutuzov smiled in a way that seemed to say: You're perfectly free not to believe me, and I really don't care whether you do or not — but you have no grounds for calling me a liar. And that's the whole point.
The Austrian general looked displeased but had no choice except to respond in the same tone.

"On the contrary," he said in a querulous, irritated voice that clashed with his flattering words, "on the contrary — Your Excellency's participation in the joint effort is highly valued by His Majesty. But we believe this current delay is robbing the splendid Russian troops and their commander of the laurels they have so often won in battle." He finished what was clearly a rehearsed speech.
Kutuzov bowed, wearing the same smile.

"But that is my conviction, and judging by the most recent letter with which His Highness Archduke Ferdinand has honored me, I would assume the Austrian forces, under the direction of so skilled a commander as General Mack, have already won a decisive victory and no longer require our assistance," said Kutuzov.

The general frowned. Although there was no confirmed news of an Austrian defeat, too many troubling rumors were circulating for comfort, and Kutuzov's cheerful mention of an Austrian victory sounded suspiciously like sarcasm. But Kutuzov went on smiling blandly with the same expression — as if he had every right to think so. And in fact, the most recent dispatch from Mack's army had reported a victory and described the army's strategic position as highly favorable.

"Let me see that letter," said Kutuzov, turning to Prince Andrew. "Have a look at this" — and with an ironic smile playing at the corners of his mouth, Kutuzov read aloud to the Austrian general the following passage, in German, from Archduke Ferdinand's letter:

We have fully concentrated forces of nearly seventy thousand men with which to attack and defeat the enemy should he cross the Lech. Also, as we command Ulm, we cannot be deprived of the advantage of holding both sides of the Danube, so that should the enemy not cross the Lech, we can cross the Danube, throw ourselves on his line of communications, recross the river further downstream, and frustrate his intentions should he try to direct his whole force against our faithful ally. We shall therefore confidently await the moment when the Imperial Russian army is fully equipped, and shall then, in conjunction with it, easily find a way to deliver the enemy the fate he deserves.
Kutuzov sighed deeply when he finished reading and looked at the Hofkriegsrath member with a mild, attentive gaze.

[speaking in French] "But you know the wise maxim, Your Excellency — always prepare for the worst," said the Austrian general, clearly wanting to move past the sarcasm and get down to business. He glanced involuntarily at the aide-de-camp.

[speaking in French] "Excuse me, General," Kutuzov interrupted, also turning to Prince Andrew. "Here's what I need, my dear fellow: get all the scout reports from Kozlovsky. Here are two letters from Count Nostitz, and here's one from His Highness Archduke Ferdinand, plus these" — he handed over several papers — "put together a clean memo in French summarizing everything we know about the Austrian army's movements, then deliver it to His Excellency."

Prince Andrew nodded to show he had understood from the first word — not only what was said, but what Kutuzov actually meant behind it. He gathered the papers and, with a bow to both men, stepped quietly across the carpet and into the anteroom.

Although not much time had passed since Prince Andrew left Russia, the change in him was remarkable. In the expression on his face, in his gestures, in the way he walked, almost no trace remained of his former mannered laziness and indifference. He now looked like a man who has no time to think about the impression he makes on others because he is absorbed in meaningful, engaging work. His face showed more contentment with himself and those around him; his smile and his eyes were brighter, more appealing.

Kutuzov, whom he had caught up with in Poland, had received him warmly, promised not to forget him, singled him out from the other adjutants, and brought him along to Vienna, entrusting him with the more important assignments. From Vienna, Kutuzov had written to his old comrade, Prince Andrew's father:
Your son gives every promise of becoming an officer distinguished by his diligence, resolve, and competence. I consider myself fortunate to have such a subordinate at my side.

On Kutuzov's staff, among his fellow officers and in the army at large, Prince Andrew had — just as in Petersburg society — two sharply opposite reputations. A minority recognized him as someone different from themselves and everyone else, expected great things of him, listened to him, admired and imitated him. With these people, Prince Andrew was natural and at ease. The majority, however, disliked him and thought him arrogant, cold, and unpleasant. But among this group, Prince Andrew knew how to carry himself in a way that commanded their respect and even their fear.
Coming out of Kutuzov's room with the papers in hand, Prince Andrew walked up to his comrade Kozlovsky, the aide-de-camp on duty, who was sitting by the window reading a book.
"Well, Prince?" Kozlovsky asked.
"I've been ordered to write a memo explaining why we aren't advancing."
"And why aren't we?"
Prince Andrew shrugged.
"Any news from Mack?"
"No."
"If he'd really been defeated, we'd have heard by now."
"Probably," said Prince Andrew, and started toward the outer door.

But at that instant, a tall Austrian general in a greatcoat strode in quickly, slamming the door behind him. He wore the Order of Maria Theresa around his neck and had a black bandage wrapped around his head. He had obviously just arrived.
"Commander in Chief Kutuzov?" the newcomer demanded, speaking quickly in a harsh German accent, looking both ways and heading straight for the inner door.
"The commander in chief is in a meeting," said Kozlovsky, hurrying up to block his path. "Whom shall I announce?"
The unknown general looked down at the rather short Kozlovsky with contempt, as if astonished that anyone could fail to recognize him.
"The commander in chief is in a meeting," Kozlovsky repeated calmly.

The general's face darkened. His lips trembled. He pulled out a notebook, scribbled something in pencil, tore out the page, thrust it at Kozlovsky, then strode to the window and threw himself into a chair, glaring around the room as if to ask: Why are they all staring at me? He raised his head and stretched his neck as though about to speak, but then, with forced indifference, began humming to himself — and the odd sound broke off almost immediately. The door to the private room opened and Kutuzov appeared in the doorway. The general with the bandaged head jerked forward as if fleeing some danger and, taking long, rapid strides on his thin legs, rushed up to Kutuzov.
[speaking in French] "You see before you the unfortunate Mack," he said in a broken voice.

Kutuzov's face, framed in the open doorway, remained completely still for several seconds. Then a wave of wrinkles passed across it, his forehead smoothed again, and he bowed his head respectfully, closed his eyes, silently let Mack walk past him into the room, and shut the door behind them both.

The rumor that the Austrians had been crushed and that the entire army had surrendered at Ulm turned out to be true. Within half an hour, adjutants were being dispatched in every direction with orders that made it clear the Russian army, inactive until now, would soon have to face the enemy.

Prince Andrew was one of those rare staff officers whose deepest interest lay in the overall course of the war. When he saw Mack and heard the details of the catastrophe, he immediately grasped that half the campaign was already lost. He vividly understood the full difficulty of the Russian army's position and could picture exactly what lay ahead and what role he would have to play. In spite of himself, he felt a surge of excitement at the thought of arrogant Austria's humiliation, and at the prospect that within a week he might witness — and take part in — the first clash between Russian and French forces since the days of Suvorov. He feared that Napoleon's genius might overwhelm Russian courage, yet at the same time he could not bear the thought of his hero being disgraced.

Agitated and unsettled by these thoughts, Prince Andrew headed to his room to write to his father, as he did every day. In the corridor he ran into Nesvitsky, with whom he shared quarters, and the joker Zherkov. As usual, they were laughing.
"Why so grim?" Nesvitsky asked, noticing Prince Andrew's pale face and glittering eyes.
"There's nothing to be cheerful about," Bolkonsky answered.

Just as Prince Andrew encountered Nesvitsky and Zherkov, two men approached from the other end of the corridor: Strauch, an Austrian general on Kutuzov's staff who oversaw provisioning for the Russian army, and the Hofkriegsrath member who had arrived the previous evening. The corridor was wide enough for the generals to pass the three officers without any difficulty, but Zherkov shoved Nesvitsky aside and said in a breathless voice:
"They're coming! They're coming! Step aside — make way, please, make way!"
The generals walked past, clearly trying to avoid any awkward attention. On Zherkov's face there suddenly appeared a stupid grin of delight that he seemed unable to suppress.
[speaking in German] "Your Excellency," he said, stepping forward and addressing the Austrian general, "I have the honor of congratulating you."
He bowed and began scraping first one foot and then the other, clumsy as a child at a dance lesson.
The Hofkriegsrath member eyed him severely, but the earnest stupidity of that beaming smile made it impossible to ignore entirely. He narrowed his eyes to show he was listening.
"I have the honor of congratulating you. General Mack has arrived — perfectly well, just a little bruised right here," Zherkov said, pointing to his own head with a radiant smile.
The general scowled, turned away, and walked on.
[speaking in German] "God, how childish!" he muttered angrily after a few steps.

Nesvitsky threw his arms around Prince Andrew with a laugh, but Bolkonsky — turning even paler — shoved him away with a furious look and rounded on Zherkov. The anxious irritation triggered by Mack's appearance, the news of his defeat, and the thought of what awaited the Russian army all found an outlet in rage at Zherkov's ill-timed joke.

"If you choose to make a buffoon of yourself, sir," he said sharply, his lower jaw trembling slightly, "I can't stop you. But I warn you: if you dare to play the fool in my presence, I will teach you how to behave."
Nesvitsky and Zherkov were so stunned by this outburst that they stared at Bolkonsky in silent, wide-eyed shock.
"What's the matter? I was only congratulating them," Zherkov said.
"I am not joking with you — be quiet!" Bolkonsky snapped, and taking Nesvitsky by the arm, he walked away from Zherkov, who stood there not knowing what to say.
"Come on, what's gotten into you?" Nesvitsky said, trying to calm him.

"What's gotten into me?" Prince Andrew burst out, stopping in his tracks, his voice shaking with emotion. "Don't you understand? Either we are officers serving our Tsar and our country, who share in its victories and grieve at its misfortunes — or we are nothing but servants who couldn't care less about their master's business. [speaking in French] Forty thousand men slaughtered and the army of our allies destroyed, and you find that amusing! [speaking in French] That's fine for some worthless nobody like that creature you've made your friend, but not for you — not for you. Only a juvenile could find entertainment in this," he added in Russian, though he used the French-accented word for juvenile, noticing that Zherkov could still hear him.
He waited a moment to see if the cornet would respond, but Zherkov turned and walked out of the corridor.

chapters.title: Book Two (1805) — Chapter V
paragraphs: The Pavlograd Hussars were stationed two miles from Braunau. The squadron in which Nikolai Rostov served as a cadet was billeted in the German village of Salzeneck. The best quarters in the village had been assigned to the squadron commander, cavalry captain Denisov, known throughout the entire cavalry division as Vaska Denisov. Cadet Rostov had been living with the squadron commander ever since catching up with the regiment in Poland.

On October 11 — the same day headquarters was buzzing with the news of Mack's defeat — life in this squadron's officers' quarters went on as usual. Denisov, who had been losing at cards all night, still hadn't come home when Rostov returned early that morning from a foraging expedition. In his cadet uniform, Rostov rode up to the porch with a jerk of the reins, swung his leg over the saddle with a supple, youthful motion, paused for a moment in the stirrup as though reluctant to part from his horse, then finally sprang down and called for his orderly.

"Ah, Bondarenko, my friend!" he said to the hussar who came running headlong toward the horse. "Walk him for me, there's a good fellow," he went on, with the open, brotherly warmth that good-natured young people radiate to everyone around them when they're happy.
"Yes, Your Excellency," the Ukrainian replied cheerfully, tossing his head.
"And make sure you walk him properly!"

Another hussar rushed toward the horse too, but Bondarenko had already looped the snaffle reins over its head. It was clear the cadet tipped generously and that serving him paid well. Rostov patted the horse's neck, then its flank, and lingered a moment longer.

"Wonderful! He's going to be a superb horse," he thought, smiling, and with his saber at his side and spurs jingling, he ran up the porch steps. His German landlord, wearing a waistcoat and a pointed cap and holding a pitchfork, was shoveling manure from the cow shed. His face brightened the moment he saw Rostov. [speaking in German] "Good morning! Very good morning!" he said, winking with a cheerful smile, clearly pleased to see the young man.

[speaking in German] "Busy already?" Rostov replied with that same bright, brotherly smile that never left his eager face. [speaking in German] "Long live Austria! Long live Russia! Long live Emperor Alexander!" he added, repeating a phrase the German landlord used constantly.
The German laughed, came out of the cow shed, pulled off his cap, and waved it over his head, shouting:
[speaking in German] "And long live the whole world!"

Rostov waved his cap in the air just like the German and laughed: [speaking in German] "And long live the whole world!" Though neither the German shoveling his cow shed nor Rostov returning from hay-gathering duty had any particular reason to rejoice, they looked at each other with joyful delight and brotherly affection, wagged their heads as a sign of mutual goodwill, and parted smiling — the German going back to his cow shed, Rostov heading to the cottage he shared with Denisov.
"Where's the master?" he asked Lavrusha, Denisov's orderly, known throughout the regiment as a rogue.

"Hasn't been back since last night. Must've been losing," Lavrusha answered. "I can always tell by now — when he wins, he comes home early to brag about it. When he stays out until morning, it means he lost, and he'll come back in a foul mood. Want coffee?"
"Yes, bring some."

Ten minutes later Lavrusha brought the coffee. "He's coming!" he announced. "Now there'll be trouble!" Rostov looked out the window and saw Denisov approaching. Denisov was a small man with a red face, sparkling black eyes, and a black tangle of mustache and hair. He wore an unbuttoned cloak, baggy trousers hanging in creases, and a crumpled shako shoved to the back of his head. He came up to the porch gloomily, his head hanging.
"Lavwuska!" he shouted, loudly and angrily. "Take this off, you blockhead!"
"I am taking it off," Lavrusha's voice came back.
"Ah — you're up already," said Denisov, walking into the room.
"Long ago," Rostov answered. "I've already been out for the hay and had a look at Fräulein Mathilde."

"Weally! And I've been losing, bwother. Lost last night like an absolute fool!" Denisov cried. He couldn't pronounce his r's. "Such wotten luck! Such wotten luck. The minute you left, it started — and it just kept going. Hey! Tea!"
Scrunching up his face in what was partly a grimace and partly a grin, showing his short, strong teeth, he began raking both sets of stubby fingers through his thick, matted black hair.

"What devil made me go to that wat?" — "the rat" being an officer's nickname — he said, rubbing his forehead and his whole face with both hands. "Can you believe it — he didn't let me win a single cahd! Not one cahd!"
He grabbed the lit pipe someone offered him, clamped it in his fist, and banged it against the floor, sending sparks flying, all while continuing to shout.
"He lets you win the singles, then snatches it back the second you double! Gives you the singles, grabs the doubles!"
He scattered the burning tobacco, smashed the pipe, and hurled it away. Then he went quiet, and suddenly looked up at Rostov with his glittering black eyes, cheerful again.

"If at least there were some women around. But there's nothing to do here but dwink. If only we could get to the fighting! Hey — who's there?" he said, turning toward the door at the sound of heavy boots, clinking spurs, and a respectful cough.
"The squadron quartermaster!" Lavrusha announced.
Denisov's face puckered even more.

"Wotten!" he muttered, tossing down a purse with some gold coins in it. "Wostov, dear fellow, count what's left and stick the purse under the pillow," he said, and went out to deal with the quartermaster.
Rostov picked up the money and, mechanically sorting the old coins from the new ones into separate piles, began counting.
"Hey, Telyanin! How are you? They cleaned me out last night," Denisov's voice came from the next room.
"Where? At Bykov's? The rat's? I knew it," a thin voice replied, and Lieutenant Telyanin — a small officer from the same squadron — walked in.

Rostov shoved the purse under the pillow and shook the moist little hand Telyanin offered. Telyanin had been transferred out of the Guards just before this campaign. He conducted himself well enough in the regiment but wasn't liked. Rostov in particular couldn't stand him, and was unable to overcome — or even hide — his baseless dislike of the man.
"Well, young cavalryman, how's my Rook doing?" Telyanin asked. Rook was a young horse he had sold to Rostov.
The lieutenant never looked directly at the person he was talking to — his eyes constantly wandered from one object to another.
"I saw you riding this morning," he added.
"Oh, he's fine — good horse," Rostov answered, even though the horse he'd paid seven hundred rubles for wasn't worth half that. "He's started going a bit lame on the left foreleg, though."
"Cracked hoof — that's nothing. I'll teach you what to do. I'll show you the right kind of rivet."
"Yes, please do," said Rostov.
"I'll show you, I'll show you. It's no secret. And you'll thank me for that horse."
"Then I'll have him brought around," said Rostov, wanting to get away from Telyanin, and he went out to give the order.

In the hallway, Denisov was squatting on the threshold with a pipe, facing the quartermaster, who was making his report. Seeing Rostov, Denisov screwed up his face, jerked his thumb over his shoulder toward the room where Telyanin sat, and gave a shudder of disgust.
"Ugh! I can't stand that fellow," he said, not caring that the quartermaster was right there.
Rostov shrugged as if to say: Neither can I, but what can you do? He gave his order and went back to Telyanin.
Telyanin sat in the same lazy posture Rostov had left him in, rubbing his small white hands.
"There really are some revolting people in this world," Rostov thought as he walked in.
"Have you told them to bring the horse?" Telyanin asked, getting up and glancing around with his usual restless casualness.
"I have."
"Let's go look ourselves. I really only stopped by to ask Denisov about yesterday's order. Did you get it, Denisov?"
"Not yet. But where are you headed?"
"I want to show this young man how to shoe a horse properly," Telyanin said.
They went through the entrance and into the stable. The lieutenant demonstrated how to set the rivet, then left for his own quarters.

When Rostov came back, there was a bottle of vodka and a sausage on the table. Denisov was sitting there, pen scratching across a sheet of paper. He looked up at Rostov gloomily and said: "I'm witing to her."
He propped his elbows on the table, pen in hand, and — clearly glad of the chance to say aloud what he wanted to put on paper — began telling Rostov the contents of his letter.

"You see, my fwiend," he said, "when we don't love, we're asleep. We're children of the dust... but the moment you fall in love — you become a god, you're as pure as on the first day of creation... Who's that now? Tell him to go to hell — I'm busy!" he shouted at Lavrusha, who came up to him without the slightest embarrassment.
"Who do you think? You told him to come yourself. It's the quartermaster — he wants the money."
Denisov frowned and started to shout something, then stopped.
"Wotten business," he muttered. "How much is left in the purse?" he asked, turning to Rostov.
"Seven new imperials and three old ones."
"Ugh — wotten! Well, what are you standing there gawking for, you scawecwow? Go call the quahtehmasteh!" he shouted at Lavrusha.
"Denisov, please — let me lend you some. I've got money, you know," said Rostov, blushing.
"Don't like bowwowing from my own comrades," Denisov growled.
"But if you won't take money from me as a friend, you'll hurt my feelings. I really do have some," Rostov insisted.
"No, I said."
Denisov went to the bed to retrieve the purse from under the pillow.
"Where did you put it, Wostov?"
"Under the bottom pillow."
"It's not here."
Denisov threw both pillows onto the floor. The purse was gone.
"That's stwange."
"Wait — maybe you dropped it?" said Rostov, picking up the pillows one by one and shaking them.
He yanked off the blanket and shook it out. No purse.
"Good lord, could I have forgotten? No — I remember thinking you were guarding it under your head like treasure," said Rostov. "I put it right here. Where is it?" He turned to Lavrusha.
"I haven't been in the room. It should be wherever you put it."
"But it's not there."
"You're always like that — you toss things down anywhere and then forget. Check your pockets."
"No — if I hadn't been thinking of it as treasure," said Rostov, "but I distinctly remember putting it there."

Lavrusha turned all the bedding inside out, looked under the bed and under the table, searched everywhere, then stood in the middle of the room and threw up his hands — it was nowhere to be found. Denisov watched Lavrusha's every move in silence, and when the orderly gave up with a helpless gesture, Denisov turned his gaze on Rostov.
"Wostov — you haven't been playing some schoolboy twick..."

Rostov felt Denisov's eyes fixed on him. He looked up and instantly dropped his gaze again. All the blood that seemed to have been pooled somewhere below his throat rushed to his face and eyes. He couldn't breathe.
"And nobody's been in the room except the lieutenant and the two of you. It has to be here somewhere," said Lavrusha.

"Now then, you little devil — get moving and find it!" Denisov shouted, suddenly turning purple and lunging at the orderly with a threatening fist. "If that purse doesn't turn up, I'll flog you — I'll flog every last one of you!"
Rostov, avoiding Denisov's eyes, began buttoning his coat, buckling on his saber, and putting on his cap.
"I want that purse, do you hear me!" Denisov bellowed, grabbing his orderly by the shoulders and slamming him against the wall.

"Denisov, leave him alone. I know who took it," said Rostov, walking toward the door without looking up. Denisov stopped, thought for a second, and — clearly understanding what Rostov was hinting at — seized his arm.

"That's nonsense!" he shouted. The veins on his forehead and neck stood out like cords. "You've lost your mind, I tell you. I won't allow it. The purse is here! I'll skin this scoundwel alive, and it'll turn up."
"I know who took it," Rostov repeated, his voice unsteady, and headed for the door.
"And I'm telling you — don't you dahe!" Denisov shouted, rushing at the cadet to hold him back.
But Rostov wrenched his arm free and, with as much fury as if Denisov were his worst enemy, fixed his eyes directly on his face.
"Do you realize what you're saying?" he asked in a shaking voice. "No one else was in this room besides me. So if the purse isn't there, then..."
He couldn't finish. He ran from the room.
"Damn it all — damn you and evewybody!" were the last words Rostov heard.
Rostov went straight to Telyanin's quarters.
"The master isn't in — he went to headquarters," Telyanin's orderly said. "Has something happened?" he added, startled by the cadet's agitated face.
"No, nothing."
"You just missed him," the orderly said.

Headquarters was two miles from Salzeneck. Without going home first, Rostov grabbed a horse and rode there. In the village there was an inn the officers frequented. Rostov rode up to it and saw Telyanin's horse tied at the porch.
In the back room of the inn, the lieutenant was sitting in front of a plate of sausages and a bottle of wine.
"Well, you've come here too, young man!" Telyanin said with a smile, raising his eyebrows.
"Yes," said Rostov, as though the word cost him enormous effort, and he sat down at the nearest table.
Neither spoke. Two Germans and a Russian officer were also in the room. Everyone was silent; the only sounds were the clatter of cutlery and Telyanin's chewing.

When Telyanin finished eating, he pulled a double purse from his pocket and, separating its rings with his small, white, upturned fingers, drew out a gold imperial. Raising his eyebrows, he handed it to the waiter.
"Quickly, please," he said.
The coin was new. Rostov stood up and walked over to Telyanin.
"May I see your purse?" he said in a low voice, barely audible.
With his eyes shifting but his eyebrows still raised, Telyanin handed over the purse.
"Yes, it's a nice purse... yes, yes," he said, suddenly turning pale. "Take a look, young man."
Rostov took the purse, examined it and the money inside, and looked at Telyanin. The lieutenant was glancing around in his usual restless way, and suddenly seemed to grow very cheerful.
"When we get to Vienna, I'll spend it there. In these miserable little towns, there's nowhere to use it," he said. "Well — let me have it back, young man. I need to go."
Rostov said nothing.
"And you? Going to have some lunch? They feed you pretty well here," Telyanin continued. "Come on, hand it over."

He reached out for the purse. Rostov released it. Telyanin took the purse and began sliding it casually into his riding breeches pocket, his eyebrows lifted and his mouth slightly open, as if to say: Yes, I'm putting my purse in my pocket — perfectly normal, nobody's business.
"Well, young man?" he said with a sigh, glancing up from under his raised brows into Rostov's eyes.
Something like an electric spark shot between Telyanin's eyes and Rostov's — back and forth, back and forth, in a single instant.
"Come here," said Rostov, grabbing Telyanin by the arm and practically dragging him to the window. "That money belongs to Denisov — you stole it," he whispered, his mouth close to Telyanin's ear.
"What? What? How dare you? What?" Telyanin sputtered.

But the words came out as a pitiful, desperate cry — a plea for forgiveness. The instant Rostov heard them, a crushing weight of doubt fell away from him. He was relieved, and at the same time he began to pity the wretched man standing before him. But what he had started had to be finished.
"God only knows what the people here might think," Telyanin muttered, grabbing his cap and moving toward a small, empty room. "We need to talk about this..."
"I know it and I'll prove it," said Rostov.
Every muscle in Telyanin's pale, terrified face was quivering. His eyes still darted from side to side, but now they stayed low, never rising to meet Rostov's. His sobs were audible.
"Count... Don't ruin a young man's life... here — here's the wretched money, take it." He threw it on the table. "I have an old father and mother!"

Rostov picked up the money, not looking at Telyanin, and walked out of the room without a word. But at the door he stopped and turned back. "My God," he said, tears in his eyes, "how could you do this?"
"Count..." Telyanin said, stepping closer.
"Don't touch me," said Rostov, pulling away. "If you need money, take it." He flung the purse at Telyanin and ran out of the inn.
